content: Destrin, also referred to as DSTN or actin depolymerizing factor (ADF), is a protein encoded by the DSTN gene in humans. It is a critical component of microfilaments and belongs to the ADF/cofilin family of actin-binding proteins. This family plays a pivotal role in enhancing the turnover of actin filaments within living cells. The DSTN gene encodes a protein that is capable of severing actin filaments (F-actin) and binding to actin monomers (G-actin). Notably, two distinct transcript variants of this gene have been identified, each encoding different isoforms of the protein. The three-dimensional structure of destrin has been elucidated using advanced triple-resonance multidimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques. Its secondary and tertiary structures bear a resemblance to those of the gelsolin family, another group of proteins involved in actin regulation. Destrin is a globular protein with a well-organized structure consisting of three distinct layers. At its core lies a β-sheet, which is composed of one parallel strand and three antiparallel strands. This β-sheet is flanked by a long α-helix and a shorter α-helix on one side, while two shorter helices are positioned on the opposite side. The four helices are oriented parallel to the β-strands, contributing to the protein's structural integrity. Functionally, destrin plays a significant role in regulating actin dynamics within the cytoskeleton of various eukaryotic cells. It binds to actin in a manner similar to the interaction observed with gelsolin segment-1. The activity of destrin, as well as that of cofilin, in binding actin is subject to negative regulation through phosphorylation. Additionally, destrin possesses the ability to sever actin filaments, further contributing to its role in actin filament turnover and cytoskeletal remodeling.
